chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
title: Tatum's reputation; Donald Lambert and Fats Waller
summary: Tatum was known to all pianists, and Fats Waller took him to meet stride pianist Donald Lambert, who was crushed by Tatum's Tiger Rag.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Art Tatum: the legend, the piano and the man

blocks.x: In Chicago you told me about all of the famous people that used to come in and line the club. But was he well known at that time in Chicago?
Oh, yes. All the pianists of classical and jazz, they knew Art Tatum.
No, outside of Chicago he was--
Oh, yes, yes, yes, yes. Well, he was an accompanist for Adelaide Hall, I believe, I think, and Fats Waller. Did I tell you this?
You mentioned something about Fats Waller and his band, but --

Oh, okay. Art often told me the story of he was appearing with Adelaide Hall as her accompanist, and Fats was on the same bill with this band. And Fats took him to New Jersey to meet a guy by the name of Donald

Lambert, who was supposed to be the king of the stride piano. And Art said that the guy really could play. He said it took him almost all night to convince this guy though, he said, and finally just after they had almost finished then he laid "Tiger Rag" on him, and that crushed him. So I got a -- and that just killed Fats. Fats sat there and he just laughed and he just enjoyed the whole thing.

I finally got a chance to meet Donald Lambert once. They did one of these jazz festivals or something, at WNEW. They used to have them yearly in New York, and Donald Lambert was there and I met him, and he could play. Stride piano. But Art was the master.
